newsitem.title: UK: Labour leader warns UK voters against complacency.
newsitem.headline: Labour leader warns UK voters against complacency.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair said on Sunday he was ready for power but warned British voters against complacency in the face of polls predicting his Labour Party would win a landslide in Thursday's election.
Labour has languished out of office for 18 years but the polls predict the main opposition party would not only win this time but win on a scale not seen for over half a century.
Four surveys in Sunday newspapers showed Labour 15 to 24 percentage points ahead of the ruling Conservatives, a lead that could produce a majority of almost 200 in a 659-seat parliament.
No party has come from so far behind in so little time to clinch victory but Blair insisted his guard was still up against a recovery by the Conservatives, in power since 1979.
"I take nothing for granted in this election," he said. "There's only one poll that counts and that's the one at election day."
He urged voters not to slip into a false sense of security and thereby hand the Conservatives a record fifth straight term.
"One of the things that we want to concentrate on in the next few days is what would happen if the Conservatives come back into power," he told BBC television.

Labour was tipped to win the last election in 1992 but its lead in the polls vanished on the day as voters stuck with the Conservatives rather than risk life under a party portrayed in a hostile media as a stooge of trade unions and enemy of the rich.
Blair has since hauled Labour to the middle ground and many papers have switched sides, saying the country needs a break from a party that is riven by infighting over ties with Europe.
The latest to switch was the best-selling Sunday newspaper, News of the World. "Britain is crying out for strong and moral leadership. John Major has provided neither," said the tabloid.
But Major -- said to be one of the few top Conservatives who still believe the election is winnable -- portrayed himself as a a pragmatic fighter who feels his government task is unfinished.

"There's no point in carrying your heart on your sleeve. You need to have an efficient, effective economy," he told ITV television. "Having got the economic background right, I'd like to carry on with the social measures."
He conceded there had been "bumps" in his leadership but accused Labour of peddling "great lies" and practicing "contemptible politics" aimed at scaring the weak.
From Major down, Conservatives have chanted a tried-and-tested message that Labour cannot be trusted on tax, trying to sow the same seed of doubt that helped them win in 1992.
"A vote for New Labour is a leap in the dark," Conservative Party Chairman Brian Mawhinney told reporters. "You can't trust Labour. If in doubt, keep them out."
But it is New Labour, by contrast to Major's party, that has maintained a strong and unified front in the six-week campaign.
Indeed, the main upset on election day might come from the Irish Republican Army amid fears of disruptive bomb threats.

The guerrilla group has posed a constant threat during the election campaign, targetting transport links and high-profile public events to sow chaos in daily life and ensure coverage for their campaign to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
Polling stations are expected to be on high alert on Thursday, with results expected early the next day.
As for his life come Friday, Blair said he was excited about the prospect of ousting Major and finally seizing power.
"Yes, I am ready. But I approach the next few days with a sense of humility and a sense of responsibility because a lot of hopes and expectations are vested in me," Blair said.
Even some Conservatives are openly tipping Labour for victory -- and saying it would not be such a bad thing either.
Outspoken Conservative MP Edwina Currie, a former minister, hit out at the campaigning style of her own party and predicted a bloodbath among the leadership after polling day.
"Tony Blair has not just talked about being tough, he has done it," she wrote in the Sunday Express paper.
Currie predicted a 100-strong Labour majority that could rise to 150-180. Labour need a uniform 4.3 percent swing to win their first election since 1974.
